with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

a## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

u## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from

page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

i## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

 ## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from

together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart

with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

r## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

crossing rather than the edge of the data.

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the

with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

 ## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

`## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

 ## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from

with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

t## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

i## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from

together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

t## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database

* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

crossing rather than the edge of the data.

with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

y## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

o## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

u## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database

* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

crossing rather than the edge of the data.

with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

t## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from

page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

r## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database

* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

crossing rather than the edge of the data.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the

with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

 ## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database

* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

crossing rather than the edge of the data.

with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

 ## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

crossing rather than the edge of the data.

with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

 ## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database

* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

crossing rather than the edge of the data.

with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.

## One question, one answer

The same verification exposed a subtler fault. The page quoted a protection
window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

window twice: 8:17 am to 3:26 pm in its own section, computed from the
clear-sky forecast, and 12:46 pm to 3:10 pm in the chart summary, computed from
the cloud-adjusted curve. Both were correct for what they measured, and
together they were useless -- two different answers to the same question on one
page, on a cloudy Perth day where the gap was four and a half hours.

The chart summary now gives the peak and says cloud is included, and quotes no
times at all. The conservative clear-sky figure is the one that should be acted
on, so it is the only one allowed to give times. A test asserts the chart
summary never contains a time range.

 ## The forecast now covers the whole local day

Resolved 25 October 2026. A CAMS 00Z run with 24 lead hours covers 00:00-23:00
UTC, which in Perth is 08:00 to 07:00 the next morning, leaving a city page
with no forecast for its own early morning. The first render duly announced
"protection needed from 11:00 am" for Sydney when the real crossing is around
8:30 -- two hours late, in the one direction this site must never err.

Two fixes, and both were needed:

* `cams.run()` requests yesterday's and today's 00Z runs with 47 lead hours
  each, so every city's local day is covered from both ends. The live database
  now holds 72 hours per city, 24 October 00Z to 26 October 23Z.
* `protectionWindow` refuses to answer unless both crossings are actually
  observed in the series, so a data boundary can never be presented as a
  crossing even if coverage regresses.

Verified against the live database: Perth reads 8:17 am to 3:26 pm, a real
crossing rather than the edge of the data.
